The third mistake - the trigger getting pulled by something in the trigger guard - wasn't really a mistake, it was just an accident. It's unusual, but it happens.

There are a couple of lessons here, might as well learn them the easy way.

The first and biggest lesson is to stop storing guns with the actions closed. I'd bet fully have the NDs I've read about happened because somebody was 'relaxing' the springs on their gun before putting it away. Modern springs don't need to be relaxed. Leave the action open because you're going to open it first thing anyway. This one small change in habit will eliminate an entire class of hazard.

Second, imagine how many people that rifle was pointed at, on his drive home from the range, bouncing over potholes. Did I mention leaving the actions open?

Third, it's the exceptional moments that kill you, those little distracted instants where little exceptions get made because we're in a hurry and thinking about something else. We rely on our habits and routines to protect us most of the time, and when we are out of the routine we are in unusual danger. Meet those moments with unusual care and things go better.
